title: Latency-bounded multi-region handoff proposal
content:
Summary
This is a design proposal for a latency-bounded multi-region handoff mechanism intended to keep client tail latency within SLOs during regional degradation. The goal is not to replace existing steering primitives (GeoDNS, Anycast, regional preference), but to define an incremental control-plane driven handoff path that: (1) detects when a region is no longer meeting latency SLOs, (2) initiates a controlled reroute of a portion or all traffic to alternative regions, and (3) preserves correctness for stateful/affinitized workloads (KV cache, model KV cache, session affinity) while bounding outage and avoiding traffic oscillation.

Motivation and constraints
- Observed issues: short-lived regional network spikes and software slowdowns produce tail spikes that exceed product latency SLOs for high-priority routes. Blind ejection of regions causes cache cold starts, spike of downstream load, and customer-visible errors.
- Hard constraints: user-visible P50/P95 must remain within configured SLOs for each route class; any handoff must complete within a bounded time window (target: 30s for full route-level redirection where possible).
- Operational constraints: minimal manual ops during incidents; allow automatic safe fallback but require human-in-the-loop for broad global changes.
- Economic: avoid unnecessary wide-area traffic duplication (i.e., don’t route everything to multiple regions unless policy/plan says so).

Key ideas (high level)
1) Fast detection from local telemetry + distributed probing: combine the control plane’s regional telemetry (latency histograms, error rates) with a lightweight active probing fabric (short p95 probes from a set of vantage points) to detect sustained SLO breaches.
2) Graded handoff vs. immediate ejection: prefer gradual weight shift (canary-style) with configurable aggressiveness, not abrupt DNS/Anycast withdraws.
3) Cache-aware handoff: warm target region caches and optionally shadow requests to maintain KV/model cache hotness before traffic cutover.
4) Safety hysteresis & heartbeat: add time windows and success thresholds to prevent flip-flops and ensure stability.
5) Bounded fallback: define a maximum-duration emergency fallback that reverts to a safe global default if control plane state becomes inconsistent.

Components and flow
- Telemetry sources: per-node tail latency & qps, route-level error rates, egress probe results, DNS health from authoritative, Anycast active measurements (RUM traces if enabled).
- Control plane decision engine: fault detector -> candidate region selector -> pacing controller -> execution plan generator.
- Execution primitives: adjust GeoDNS weights (TTL-limited), update Anycast BGP pref/withdraw (where under our control), control-plane per-customer steering weights (route-level), and orchestration hooks for cache warming/shadowing.
- Observability surface: per-change audit, roll-forward/rollback buttons in Console, and real-time impact dashboard (requests shifted, p95/p99, cache hit ratio in target region).

Detection heuristics (detailed)
- Short circuit: if node-level health signals (OOM, process crash, critical infra alarms) present, trigger immediate emergency ejection path (fast but conservative).
- Latency SLO breach: combine the following over a sliding 1m and 5m window: (a) p95 above configured threshold, (b) p99 rising trend > 2x baseline, (c) error rate increase above baseline by x% (configurable). Use weighted scoring; require score > threshold to trigger candidate selection.
- Probe confirmation: after a local score crosses threshold, the decision engine kicks probes from 3 distinct vantage pools (edge POPs, control-plane agents in other regions, synthetic external probes). If >50% of probes to the target region show elevated latency, escalate. Probe windows are short (6–12s) to keep detection fast.

Candidate selection and ranking
- For each route, produce a ranked list of fallback regions based on: (1) proximity SLO delta, (2) current spare capacity (estimated from cluster util and active autoscale headroom), (3) model variant compatibility (same quantization/version), (4) cost policy (prefer lower-cost eligible regions only if they meet latency), (5) regional compliance constraints.
- If no single region satisfies constraints, consider split-path: selective routing by customer tier or token class (e.g., route 10% of best-effort traffic to other regions, keep premium on original region).

Pacing controller and cache warming
- Pacing controller: shifts traffic in small steps (configurable step size, default 10% every 6s) with success checks after each step (latency & error gates). This smooths utilization and reduces cold-start shock.
- Cache warming: before shifting more than 20% traffic, optionally enable request-shadowing to the selected region(s) for warm-up (no user-facing response) or proactively prefetch popular prefixes into model KV caches. For model-serving, warm top-k token prefixes from recent traces to avoid immediate KV miss storms.

Consistency and affinity handling
- Affinity labeling: routes may have affinity labels (session-cookie, client-ip, token-lease). Handoff logic respects affinity by attempting to keep existing sessions anchored for a short lease (e.g., 2–5 minutes) and only redirect new sessions first.
- Sticky circuits: provide a configurable sticky timeout where clients are not immediately moved; this reduces active session disruption but may slow SLA remediation—document tradeoffs.

Safety (hysteresis and rollback)
- Two-phase commit for major changes: generate execution plan -> pre-checks (capacity & cache warming) -> apply incremental weights -> validate metrics -> mark complete. If at any step metrics breach rollback thresholds (e.g., p95 increases >20% over pre-change), automatically revert to last known-good config.
- Circuit breaker: if the target region fails validation during pacing, freeze the control-plane decision and mark region as candidate for temporary ejection.
- Manual override: console button labeled "force ejection" that skips warm-up for critical emergencies, but gated by RBAC and must append incident ticket ID.

Edge interaction: GeoDNS vs. Anycast vs. Direct control-plane routing
- GeoDNS (TTL-based): use for coarse weight shifts for clients that respect DNS TTL and are not Anycast-bound. Keep low TTLs during incidents to accelerate convergence for new clients, but watch DNS query amplification and downstream resolver caching.
- Anycast: when we control the Anycast plane, prefer to shift BGP communities or withdraw prefixes for fast cutover for bulk traffic, but only after evaluating inter-region bandwidth and ARP/bgp convergence windows with infra.
- Control-plane per-tenant steering: for customers on dedicated capacity or private deployments, directly adjust per-tenant routing at the control plane layer to avoid DNS unpredictability.

Operational playbooks and runbook snippets
- Detection -> Triage flow: when telemetry triggers, the system opens an incident stub with recommended candidate regions and a suggested pacing plan. SRE reviews within 60s and can accept/adjust plan.
- Emergency ejection: if crash-loop or severe infra failure, runforce-eject (console override). Post-mortem must include: why warm-up was skipped, downstream impact, and cache regeneration cost estimate.
- Post-handoff recovery: once region recovers, reintroduce it via slow ramp (reverse pacing) and rewarm caches if necessary—do not auto-reinstate to full weight without confirmation.

Testing and validation plan
- Offline simulation harness: extend existing steering sim to test pacing parameters under synthetic load and cache models. Run chaos experiments (simulate slow node pool, packet loss) to verify time-to-SLO and cache hit impacts.
- Canary in prod: stage 1: internal-only routes, stage 2: low-traffic public routes, stage 3: broad rollout after 3 successful incidents without operator override.
- Metrics to validate: handoff completion time, p50/p95/p99 before/after, cache miss rate delta, additional inter-region bandwidth used, and rollback frequency.

Open questions / trade-offs
- How aggressive should automatic ejection be for premium customers? Recommend a policy matrix separating premium (manual or conservative auto) vs. free-tier (aggressive auto).
- Cost vs. latency: warming and shadowing increases cross-region bandwidth—should be limited by budget policies per customer/route.
- DNS TTL collision with large public resolver caches meaning GeoDNS convergence might be much slower for certain clients—fallback to Anycast or per-client control-plane overrides when consistency is critical.

Next steps (short term)
1. Prototype decision engine module in steering control plane (PLAT-8721).
2. Integrate a small set of synthetic probe agents in 3 edge POPs and wire into telemetry pipeline.
3. Implement pacing controller with configurable step size and success gates, expose in Console under route-level rollout settings.
4. Run a set of sims and two controlled chaos tests to validate parameters.

Appendix: quick parameter defaults (initial)
- detection window: 1m fast, 5m stability check
- probe confirmation: 3 vantage pools, 60% fail threshold
- pacing step: 10% traffic shifts per 6s, max 6 steps (60%) without cache warming
- cache-warm threshold: enable shadowing before shifting >20%
- sticky session lease: 180s default for affinitized routes

Notes and references
- Related: see CONFLUENCE: RW-PLAT/hand-off-spec and GH PR #145 for early implementation sketch.
- Incident examples and previous lessons learned are in the incident repo referenced in PLAT-8721.
